chunks: "Temperature affects a LiPo in pretty much every way, and it's asymmetric.
In the cold, the electrolyte gets more viscous and the reactions slow down, so the internal resistance goes up a lot.
As a rough model, it goes up about two and a half times at 0 degrees C and maybe five to six times at minus 20, compared to room temperature.
The same current then gives a bigger I R drop, so the voltage sags more, the cell hits the cutoff early, and you only get a fraction of the rated capacity.
For a 2 amp-hour cell at 1C my model says about 1. 95 amp-hours at 25 degrees but only about 1. 6 at 0 and well under half at minus 20.
That is mostly reversible; warm it up and it comes back. The bigger deal is charging in the cold.
Below about 0 degrees, lithium can't intercalate into the graphite fast enough, so it plates as metal, and that is permanent and can cause shorts.
So chargers use an NTC to block charging outside roughly 0 to 45 degrees.

In the heat it's the opposite: resistance drops so performance looks great, but aging accelerates, gas generation increases, and above about 60 degrees you're approaching the region where safety margins vanish.
So in practice you monitor temperature, limit charge current outside the sweet spot, and design thermally."
